questions.q: You and Om both want to be the train driver in a game. What is fair?
o: Om drives because he is bigger
You drive because you asked first loudly
questions.why: Taking turns lets both of you enjoy the game.

questions.q: A new boy, Neel, doesn't know anyone. What can you do?
o: Ask him to sit with you
Wait for him to come to you
Tell him the class rules strictly
questions.why: Inviting a new child helps him make a friend fast.

questions.q: Your friend is talking. When should you speak?
o: As soon as you remember something
While your friend is still talking
Only if the teacher says so
questions.why: Waiting for a friend to finish shows you are listening.

questions.q: You want to play with Diya's doll. What should you do?
o: Ask, "Can I play with it, please?"
Take it while she is not looking
Hold it and say "I'm only looking"
Ask her mother instead of her
questions.why: Asking first shows respect for her things.

questions.q: Your team is building a sandcastle. What makes the team work well?
o: Everyone gets a job to do
One child does it all alone
questions.why: When everyone has a job, the team builds better together.

questions.q: Your friend says "thank you" to you. What do you say back?
questions.why: Saying "You're welcome" is the polite reply.

questions.q: You bumped into someone in the line. What do you say?
questions.why: Saying sorry and checking on them is good manners.

questions.q: Two friends are fighting over a ball. What is a good idea?
o: Suggest playing a game with the ball together
Pick the friend you like more
Tell them to stop being friends
questions.why: Playing together turns a fight into fun.

questions.q: Your class is playing a game and you lose. What do you say to the winner?
questions.why: Congratulating the winner is good sportsmanship.

questions.q: Dadi is speaking to you. Where should you look?
questions.why: Looking at someone shows you are listening.

questions.q: A friend is sitting alone during games. What can you say?
questions.why: Inviting someone in makes them feel welcome.

questions.q: You and Kiara both want the same book in the library. What is fair?
o: One reads it first and then gives it to the other
Hide it so you can read it later
Ask the librarian to throw it away
questions.why: Taking turns with the book is fair to both.

questions.q: Your friend drops her crayons. What can you do?
o: Tell her to be careful next time
questions.why: Helping out is what good friends do.

questions.q: You are playing and a younger child wants to join. What can you do?
o: Give them an easy job in the game
Say the game is only for big kids
Let them watch from the side
Tell them to come back next year
questions.why: Giving younger kids a job lets them join safely.

questions.q: When you meet your teacher in the morning, what can you say?
o: Nothing, she knows you are here
questions.why: Greeting people is polite and friendly.

questions.q: Your friend tells you a joke that isn't funny to you. What can you do?
o: Smile and say "Tell me another one!"
Tell a better joke to show them
questions.why: Being kind about a joke keeps your friend happy.

questions.q: You need the glue but Rohan is using it. What do you say?
o: "Can I use the glue when you finish?"
questions.why: Asking politely and waiting is respectful.

questions.q: In a group game, what should everyone do with the rules?
o: Make up new rules when losing
Let the best player skip rules
questions.why: Same rules for everyone makes the game fair.

questions.q: Your neighbour aunty gives you a sweet. What do you say?
questions.why: Saying thank you shows good manners.

questions.q: Your friend is on crutches and can't run. What game could you choose?
o: A game everyone can play sitting down
Hide and seek in the park
questions.why: Choosing a game everyone can play includes your friend.

questions.q: You see a classmate drop their tiffin. What is kind?
o: Help them and share some of your food
questions.why: Helping and sharing makes your classmate feel cared for.

questions.q: Your team scored a goal because of Imran's pass. What can you say?
questions.why: Saying "great pass" shares the credit with your teammate.

questions.q: You want to join two friends who are drawing. What can you say?
questions.why: Asking to join is friendly and polite.

questions.q: Your little cousin is visiting. What can you do to be a good host?
o: Show your toys and share them
Watch TV and let them sit
questions.why: Sharing your things makes a guest feel welcome.

questions.q: In class, someone is speaking. What is good listening?
o: Look at them and stay quiet
questions.why: Good listeners look and stay quiet.

questions.q: Your friend's tower fell down. What can you say?
questions.why: Offering to help shows you are a good friend.

questions.q: You promised to share your colours with Pari but you forgot. What should you do?
o: Say sorry and share them now
questions.why: Keeping promises, even late, builds trust.

questions.q: A child in your class speaks a different language at home. What is a kind thing?
o: Ask them to teach you a word
Tell them to speak only your language
questions.why: Learning from each other makes friends.

questions.q: Your group has one swing. How many turns should each child get?
questions.why: Equal turns are fair for everyone.

questions.q: Your friend is shy. How can you help her join the game?
o: Hold her hand and bring her in
Tell her she is too shy
questions.why: A gentle hand helps a shy friend feel brave.

questions.q: Your teacher asks the class to clean up. What should you do?
o: Help clean, even things you didn't use
Wait for others to do it
questions.why: Helping the class clean shows teamwork.

questions.q: You and your brother broke a vase together. What should you both do?
o: Tell Mumma together and say sorry
questions.why: Owning up together is honest and fair.

questions.q: A friend has a new haircut. What is a kind thing to say?
questions.why: Kind words make friends feel happy.

questions.q: It's your friend's turn in a game but they don't notice. What do you do?
o: Wait and see if they notice
questions.why: Reminding them keeps the game fair.

questions.q: You find a lost pencil box in class. What should you do?
o: Keep it if no one asks
questions.why: Giving lost things to the teacher helps them go back to their owner.

questions.q: You want to sit in the front seat but so does your sister. What's fair?
o: Take turns, one on the way there, one on the way back
The one who runs first gets it
Sit there and refuse to move
questions.why: Taking turns is fair to both.

questions.q: Your friend wins a prize. How can you show you are happy for them?
questions.why: Clapping and cheering shows you are happy for them.

questions.q: In a team relay, your teammate drops the baton. What do you say?
questions.why: Encouraging teammates helps the team keep going.

questions.q: A child asks to borrow your eraser. What can you do?
o: Lend it and ask for it back after
Say you need it all day
questions.why: Lending things kindly helps classmates.

questions.q: Your friend talks about her pet cat. How do you show you are listening?
o: Ask a question about the cat
Talk about your dog right away
questions.why: Asking a question shows you care about what they said.

questions.q: Someone is waiting to pass through the door. What can you do?
questions.why: Holding the door is polite and helpful.

questions.q: Your class has a group song. One child sings off-tune. What do you do?
questions.why: Being kind keeps the group happy and together.

questions.q: Your friend brings a lunch you have never seen. What can you say?
questions.why: Being curious and kind about others' food is respectful.

questions.q: You and your friend want to play different games. What is a fair idea?
o: Play one game first, then the other
questions.why: Doing both games one after another is fair.

questions.q: An older child is teasing a younger child. What should you do?
questions.why: Telling a grown-up helps stop teasing safely.

questions.q: You are going to a friend's home. What should you say when you leave?
questions.why: Thanking your hosts is good manners.

questions.q: Your friend can't open her water bottle. What do you do?
o: Tell her to ask the teacher
questions.why: Helping with small things shows kindness.

questions.q: In a game, you see your friend cheating. What should you say?
questions.why: Calmly asking to follow rules keeps the game fair.

questions.q: Your friend wants to tell you something but you're busy. What do you say?
o: "Can you tell me in five minutes?"
questions.why: Asking for a little time is kind and honest.

questions.q: You see a classmate who looks lost on sports day. What can you do?
o: Ask, "Can I help you find your group?"
questions.why: Helping someone who is lost is kind.

questions.q: Your friend lends you a book. How should you return it?
o: In good shape, and say thank you
questions.why: Taking care of borrowed things shows respect.

questions.q: In a group drawing, everyone wants the red colour. What can you do?
o: Break it so everyone gets a piece
questions.why: Sharing in turns lets everyone use the red.

questions.q: A friend is telling a story. You know how it ends. What do you do?
questions.why: Letting them finish is polite.

questions.q: Two children in your class are always left out of games. What can you do?
o: Invite them to play with you
Tell them to make their own game
questions.why: Inviting them makes them feel part of the group.

questions.q: You and a friend made a mess together. What should you do?
questions.why: Cleaning up together is fair.

questions.q: Your grandfather is telling an old story. What can you do?
questions.why: Listening to elders shows respect.

questions.q: Your friend's birthday is today. What could you do?
o: Wish them and make a small card
questions.why: Wishing friends on their birthday makes them happy.

questions.q: Someone in your class said sorry to you. What can you say?
o: "Thank you for saying sorry. It's okay."
questions.why: Accepting an apology helps friends make up.

questions.q: At a party, there is one big cake. How should it be cut?
o: So everyone gets a fair piece
Biggest piece for the birthday child only
questions.why: Fair pieces mean everyone enjoys the cake.

questions.q: You want to talk but your mother is on the phone. What do you do?
o: Wait, or quietly touch her arm and wait
questions.why: Waiting politely shows good manners.

questions.q: Your group project has one member who isn't doing their share. What's the best first step?
o: Talk to them privately and ask what's getting in the way
Do their part and complain later
Tell the teacher immediately without speaking to them
Remove their name from the project
questions.why: A private conversation can reveal a problem you can solve together.

questions.q: You're new to a class where everyone already has friends. What's a good way to fit in?
o: Join a club or activity where you share interests
Act like you don't need friends
questions.why: Shared interests are an easy way to make friends.

questions.q: Two friends ask you to choose sides in their fight. What's best?
o: Stay neutral and encourage them to talk to each other
Choose the friend you know longer
Tell each one what the other said
questions.why: Staying neutral helps you keep both friendships and helps them sort it out.

questions.q: In a group discussion, one person keeps talking over others. As a leader, what do you do?
o: Politely say, "Let's hear from everyone," and invite others in
Let them talk since they have ideas
Tell them to be quiet in front of all
questions.why: Fair leaders make space for every voice.

questions.q: You disagree with your teammate's plan for the science fair. What's a respectful approach?
o: Say what you like about it, then suggest your change with reasons
Go along with it and complain later
questions.why: Starting with what you like makes people open to suggestions.

questions.q: A classmate from another state is teased for their accent. What should you do?
o: Support them and tell the teasers it's not okay
Laugh so you don't get teased too
Advise them to change their accent
questions.why: Standing up for others builds a respectful class.

questions.q: You're the captain and your team lost. What should you say to the team?
o: "We played hard. Let's learn and improve for next time."
"We lost because of a few people."
"I don't want to talk about it."
questions.why: A good captain lifts the team and focuses on improvement.

questions.q: Your friend shares something private with you. What should you do?
o: Keep it private unless someone could get hurt
Use it in a joke later
questions.why: Keeping confidences builds trust, except when safety is at risk.

questions.q: You see someone sitting alone at the canteen. What can you do?
o: Invite them to join your table
Wait for them to come over
Assume they want to be alone
questions.why: Small invitations help others feel included.

questions.q: Your team has to choose a project topic but everyone wants different ones. What's fair?
o: List the ideas and vote, or combine the best ones
questions.why: Voting or combining ideas is a fair way for a group to decide.

questions.q: A friend borrowed money and hasn't returned it. What's best?
o: Remind them politely and ask when they can pay
Tell everyone they don't pay back
questions.why: A polite reminder respects the friendship.

questions.q: You notice your classmate is struggling with English. How can you help?
o: Speak to them only in English slowly
questions.why: Practising together builds skill and friendship.

questions.q: You've been asked to plan a class party. How do you include everyone?
o: Ask classmates for ideas about food, games and music
Invite only your friends to plan
Keep it a secret surprise from everyone
questions.why: Asking for ideas makes everyone feel part of it.

questions.q: Your friend is upset because you didn't reply to their message. What's best?
o: Apologise and explain you got busy
Say you don't have to reply
questions.why: Honest explanations keep trust.

questions.q: A teacher asks a question and a shy classmate gives a wrong answer. Others laugh. What can you do?
o: Not laugh, and say something encouraging later
questions.why: Encouragement helps shy classmates keep trying.

questions.q: In a team game, your friend wants to play but isn't very good. What's the best approach?
o: Include them and help them improve
Let them play only when winning
questions.why: Including friends and helping them is good team spirit.

questions.q: You disagree with a rule your friends made in a game. What do you do?
o: Explain your reason and suggest a fair change
Ignore the rule and play your way
questions.why: Suggesting changes calmly helps the group agree.

questions.q: Your friend says something rude to your sibling. What's best?
o: Tell your friend calmly that it isn't okay
Never talk to your friend again
questions.why: Calmly standing up for family shows respect.

questions.q: You're in a group chat where people are being mean about someone. What do you do?
o: Say it isn't kind and stop it there
questions.why: Speaking up can stop online meanness.

questions.q: Your team won because of someone else's great play. What's right?
o: Give them credit in front of everyone
Say it was team effort and move on
questions.why: Giving credit openly is fair and builds team spirit.

questions.q: You need help with homework but feel embarrassed to ask. What's best?
o: Ask a friend or teacher politely
questions.why: Asking for help is smart and normal.

questions.q: A friend is always late to group meetings. What's a good way to handle it?
o: Agree on a time together and send a reminder
questions.why: Agreeing on times and reminders solves the problem kindly.

questions.q: You see a classmate drop money without noticing. What should you do?
o: Pick it up and give it back
Keep it if no one saw
Give it to the teacher at the end of term
Tell others to look for it
questions.why: Returning things is honest and builds trust.

questions.q: Your friend has different beliefs and festivals from yours. What's respectful?
o: Learn about their festivals and wish them
Ask them to celebrate yours instead
questions.why: Learning about others' traditions builds respect.

questions.q: You're leading a group and one member's idea is weak. What's a kind response?
o: Thank them and ask how it could be improved
questions.why: Valuing every idea keeps people contributing.

questions.q: Your friends want to prank a teacher. You don't feel okay. What do you do?
o: Say you're not comfortable and suggest something else
questions.why: Saying no politely shows respect and courage.

questions.q: You are on a team where people speak different home languages. How do you communicate well?
o: Use simple shared words and check everyone understood
Let only the best speakers talk
questions.why: Checking understanding helps everyone take part.

questions.q: A classmate keeps copying your work. What should you do?
o: Tell them politely you'd rather help them understand it
Tell the teacher at once without speaking to them
questions.why: Offering to help solves the problem and keeps things fair.

questions.q: At a family function, an older relative asks about your marks. You feel uncomfortable. What's polite?
o: Answer briefly and change the topic kindly
questions.why: Polite short answers respect elders and your comfort.

questions.q: Your friend apologises after a fight. What's a good response?
o: Accept it and talk about how to avoid it next time
questions.why: Accepting and planning ahead repairs friendships.

questions.q: In a group, someone keeps making all the decisions. What can you say?
o: "Can we hear everyone's ideas before deciding?"
questions.why: Polite suggestions make groups fairer.

questions.q: Your class is collecting donations. What's a good way to help?
o: Help collect and organise, whatever you can give
Give the most to show off
Tell others what they should give
questions.why: Helping in any way is valuable.

questions.q: Your friend is being bullied but asks you not to tell. What should you do?
o: Tell a trusted adult because their safety matters
questions.why: Safety matters more than secrets.

questions.q: You meet an elderly neighbour who seems lonely. What can you do?
o: Chat with them sometimes and offer small help
questions.why: Small visits can make a big difference.

questions.q: Two classmates aren't speaking after a fight. You're friends with both. What helps?
o: Encourage them to talk and listen to each other
questions.why: Encouraging direct talk helps them make up.

questions.q: You notice a classmate has no partner for a project. What do you do?
o: Invite them to join your group
Wait for the teacher to sort it
questions.why: Inviting them prevents them feeling left out.

questions.q: Your friend lies to you. You feel hurt. What's the best approach?
o: Tell them how it made you feel and ask why
questions.why: Honest talk helps friends understand each other.

questions.q: During a match, the referee makes a wrong call against your team. What's best?
o: Accept it and keep playing well
questions.why: Accepting decisions shows good sportsmanship.

questions.q: You and your sibling share a room. How can you avoid fights?
o: Agree on simple room rules together
Divide the room with tape and never cross it
questions.why: Agreeing on rules together prevents arguments.

questions.q: Someone in your class has a disability. How can you be a good classmate?
o: Treat them as a friend and ask if they want help
Help with everything even if they don't need it
questions.why: Respect means friendship and asking before helping.

questions.q: Your friend shares a video that makes fun of a group of people. What should you do?
o: Say you don't find it funny and don't share it
Report your friend to the police
questions.why: Not spreading hurtful content shows respect for everyone.

questions.q: You're working in pairs and your partner is much faster than you. What helps?
o: Ask them to explain their method
Ask the teacher to change partners
questions.why: Learning from a partner helps you both.

questions.q: Your friend forgot your birthday. What's the best response?
o: Tell them lightly it was your birthday
questions.why: Gentle honesty lets friends make it up to you.

questions.q: In a debate, your opponent makes a good point. What should you do?
o: Acknowledge it and respond with your own point
questions.why: Acknowledging good points shows respect and confidence.

questions.q: You've been chosen to welcome guests at an event. What makes a good impression?
o: Smile, greet them, and guide them to their seats
Talk only to people you know
questions.why: Warm greetings make guests feel welcome.

questions.q: Your classmates are planning a trip, and one can't afford it. What can the group do?
o: Plan a cheaper trip that everyone can join
Tell them to ask their parents
questions.why: Inclusive planning makes sure no one is left out.

questions.q: You see your friend copying in an exam. What's right?
o: Tell the teacher quietly, and talk to your friend afterwards
Copy too, so it's fair for you
questions.why: Cheating is unfair to everyone; telling the teacher quietly and talking to your friend is the honest way.

questions.q: A teammate made a mistake that cost you a point. What's best to say?
o: "No problem, we'll get the next one!"
Ask the coach to replace them
questions.why: Encouraging words keep the team strong.

questions.q: You and your friend want different things for a joint gift for your teacher. What's fair?
o: Combine ideas or choose one together
Let your friend decide and complain
questions.why: Deciding together is fair and keeps the friendship.

questions.q: Your neighbour's dog keeps barking. What's a polite way to handle it?
o: Ask your parents to talk kindly with the neighbour
Complain to everyone in the building
questions.why: Polite conversations solve neighbour issues.

questions.q: You're asked to show a new student around school. What's helpful?
o: Show the key places and introduce them to friends
Tell them to follow the map
questions.why: A good tour plus friends helps a new student settle in.

questions.q: A friend tells you about a problem at home. What's supportive?
o: Listen and suggest they talk to a trusted adult if needed
Give lots of advice right away
questions.why: Listening and pointing to support helps without overstepping.

questions.q: Your team keeps losing because members don't pass the ball. What can help?
o: Talk as a team about passing and practise it
questions.why: Talking and practising together improves teamwork.

questions.q: You are invited to two parties on the same day. What's polite?
o: Choose one and politely thank the other host
Say yes to both and go to one
questions.why: Being honest and polite respects both hosts.

questions.q: Your class has a student who often interrupts. How can the class help?
o: Agree on a hand-raising rule for everyone
questions.why: Shared rules help everyone take turns fairly.

questions.q: Your friend is nervous about singing on stage. What can you do?
o: Practise with them and cheer from the front
Tell them they'll be fine and leave
questions.why: Practice and support help nervous friends shine.

questions.q: Your group finished early and another group is struggling. What could you do?
o: Offer to help them if the teacher agrees
questions.why: Helping others is good teamwork.

questions.q: Your friend is angry with you for something you didn't do. What's best?
questions.why: Calm explanations clear up misunderstandings.

questions.q: At the bus stop, an elderly person is standing. You have a seat on the bus. What should you do?
o: Ask someone else to give up their seat
questions.why: Offering your seat is respectful and kind.

questions.q: Your teacher asks for volunteers. You're unsure but interested. What's good?
o: Wait for others to go first
questions.why: Volunteering builds skills and confidence.

questions.q: A friend shares a different opinion about a sports team. What's respectful?
o: Discuss it in a friendly way
questions.why: Friendly discussion keeps friendships fun.

questions.q: Your classmate is always last to be chosen for teams. What can you do?
o: Choose them early when you're captain
questions.why: Choosing them early shows inclusion.

questions.q: You promised to meet a friend but can't make it. What should you do?
o: Tell them early and suggest another time
questions.why: Telling early shows respect for their time.

questions.q: Your friends are making plans that leave out someone. What do you say?
questions.why: Speaking up for inclusion makes your group kinder.

questions.q: A shopkeeper gave you extra change by mistake. What should you do?
questions.why: Returning it is honest and fair.

questions.q: Your partner in a science project has a different idea for the experiment. What's best?
o: Try both ideas if possible and compare results
questions.why: Testing both ideas is fair and scientific.

questions.q: A stranger asks you for directions in your neighbourhood. What do you do?
o: Explain from where you are, and never go with them or get into a vehicle
Walk with them to the place so they don't get lost
Get into their car to show the way
questions.why: You can help by explaining, but staying where you are keeps you safe.

questions.q: A friend says, "You always choose the game." What's a good response?
questions.why: Listening to feedback and sharing choices is fair.

questions.q: You're leading a school committee where two members clash constantly. What's the most effective approach?
o: Meet them together, set shared goals and clear roles
Ignore it and hope it settles
Side with the one with better ideas
questions.why: Clear goals and roles reduce conflict and refocus the team.

questions.q: A friend often shares your achievements as if they were their own. What's best?
o: Talk privately and explain how it makes you feel
questions.why: A private, honest talk protects the friendship.

questions.q: In a group project, everyone agrees except one person who raises a valid concern. What should the group do?
o: Pause and consider the concern seriously
Ask them to stop being negative
Move on and fix problems later
questions.why: Good teams listen to concerns before deciding.

questions.q: You're asked to give feedback on a friend's essay that is weak. What's the most helpful way?
o: Point out strengths first, then specific improvements
Say it's great to avoid hurting them
questions.why: Balanced, specific feedback helps them improve.

questions.q: You notice a classmate from a different background being excluded. What's a meaningful action?
o: Include them in your group and activities
Tell the teacher and do nothing else
Wait for them to make friends
questions.why: Direct inclusion makes a real difference.

questions.q: Your team is divided on a decision and time is short. What's a good leadership move?
o: Summarise options, set a quick vote, and commit together
Make the decision alone without explanation
questions.why: Quick, fair processes help teams decide under pressure.

questions.q: A friend constantly cancels at the last minute. What's the most mature response?
o: Talk to them about the pattern and agree on a plan
questions.why: Addressing patterns directly is fair and mature.

questions.q: In an online discussion, someone posts a strong opinion you disagree with. What's best?
o: Reply respectfully with facts, or choose not to engage
questions.why: Respectful disagreement keeps discussions healthy.

questions.q: You're new in a college hostel and roommates have different habits. What helps?
o: Agree on shared rules early, like quiet hours
questions.why: Early agreements prevent conflicts.

questions.q: During a team presentation, a teammate forgets their part. What do you do?
o: Smoothly help by picking up the point
questions.why: Supporting teammates on the spot keeps the team strong.

questions.q: A friend is spreading a rumour about someone you know. What's right?
o: Tell your friend you won't spread it and why
Pass it on to a few people
Warn the person but share the rumour too
questions.why: Refusing to spread rumours stops harm.

questions.q: You're elected class representative. How should you represent everyone?
o: Collect views from all classmates, not just friends
Share your own views as class views
Represent those who voted for you
questions.why: A fair representative listens to everyone.

questions.q: You notice a teammate is doing more work than others. What can you do?
o: Raise it in the team and share tasks fairly
questions.why: Fair work-sharing keeps teams healthy.

questions.q: Your friend asks you to lie for them to their parents. What's best?
o: Say you can't lie but will support them in being honest
Agree but tell their parents later
questions.why: Supporting honesty protects trust and the friendship.

questions.q: You and a classmate strongly disagree about a social issue. What's a good way to talk?
o: Listen to understand their view, then share yours
questions.why: Understanding first leads to better conversations.

questions.q: You join a club where seniors dominate decisions. How can you contribute?
o: Offer ideas respectfully and volunteer for tasks
Stay quiet until you're a senior
questions.why: Respectful contributions earn trust and influence.

questions.q: A group of friends wants to exclude someone from a trip. What's the right move?
questions.why: Speaking up for fairness is brave and right.

questions.q: Your teammate has a good idea but is too shy to share it. What can you do?
o: Encourage them and help them present it
Tell them to speak up themselves
questions.why: Helping others share ideas builds a better team.

questions.q: A classmate asks for your notes right before an exam, but they never help others. What's fair?
o: Share if you can, and kindly ask them to help others too
questions.why: Fairness and kindness can go together.

questions.q: You hear a friend make a stereotype about a group. What's an effective response?
o: Calmly question the stereotype with an example
Lecture them in front of others
questions.why: Calm questioning helps people rethink stereotypes.

questions.q: You are organising an inter-school event. What's key to working with other schools?
o: Clear communication and respecting their ideas
questions.why: Respectful communication builds partnerships.

questions.q: Two close friends are in a conflict and both vent to you. What's best?
o: Listen to both but avoid taking sides
Share what each says with the other
questions.why: Neutral listening supports both without making things worse.

questions.q: You see someone being mocked for their appearance online. What's an effective action?
o: Report the post and privately support the person
Share it to show how bad it is
questions.why: Reporting and support help without spreading harm.

questions.q: Your project partner keeps missing deadlines. What's the best step?
o: Discuss the issue and agree on clear smaller deadlines
questions.why: Clear, smaller deadlines help partners stay on track.

questions.q: At a family gathering, relatives argue about politics. What can you do?
o: Stay respectful and gently suggest a lighter topic
questions.why: Gently redirecting keeps family gatherings peaceful.

questions.q: You're mentoring a younger student. What makes you a good mentor?
o: Listen, guide, and let them make their own choices
Tell them exactly what to do
questions.why: Good mentors guide while building independence.

questions.q: You notice that only a few people speak during class discussions. As a student leader, what could you suggest?
o: Small group talks before sharing with the class
questions.why: Small groups help everyone participate.

questions.q: A friend is upset because you spent time with another group. What's the best approach?
o: Reassure them and include them next time
questions.why: Reassurance and inclusion keep friendships secure.

questions.q: You're asked to work with someone you don't like. What's professional?
o: Focus on the task and treat them respectfully
questions.why: Respectful teamwork matters even with people you don't like.

questions.q: Your group wins an award, but one quiet member did a lot behind the scenes. What should you do?
o: Accept the award as a group only
questions.why: Public credit shows fairness and gratitude.

questions.q: You realise you dominated a conversation. What's a good fix?
o: Ask others questions and listen more
questions.why: Inviting others in balances the conversation.

questions.q: You see a classmate cheating in a competitive exam. What's the right action?
o: Report it to the invigilator discreetly
questions.why: Discreet reporting keeps things fair for everyone.

questions.q: A friend asks for your honest opinion on their outfit for an event. What's best?
o: Say it's perfect no matter what
questions.why: Honesty with kindness helps friends.

questions.q: During a group trip, someone feels sick. What's the most responsible step?
o: Inform the teacher and stay with them
Call their parents without telling the teacher
questions.why: Informing the responsible adult is the safe choice.

questions.q: You join a sports team where seniors haze juniors. What's right?
o: Refuse to take part and report it to a coach
questions.why: Refusing and reporting stops harmful behaviour.

questions.q: A teammate disagrees with you in front of the coach. What's the best response?
o: Discuss calmly and respect the coach's decision
questions.why: Calm discussion keeps the team united.

questions.q: Your friends often joke about someone's poverty. What's best?
o: Tell them it's hurtful and change the topic
Join in with your own joke
questions.why: Calmly naming hurt can change group behaviour.

questions.q: You're unsure how to greet someone from a different culture. What's a respectful approach?
o: Follow their lead or politely ask
Use your usual greeting no matter what
questions.why: Asking or following their lead shows respect.

questions.q: A peer asks you to help them write their assignment fully. What's right?
o: Help them understand it but let them write it
questions.why: Helping them learn is fair and honest.

questions.q: Your team needs to present but one member is very anxious. What's supportive?
o: Give them a part they're comfortable with
questions.why: Matching roles to comfort supports everyone.

questions.q: Someone in a meeting is being interrupted repeatedly. What could you say?
questions.why: Small interventions protect people's voices.

questions.q: You're organising a class reunion. Some classmates have lost touch. What's inclusive?
o: Make an effort to contact everyone
Invite only those you're friends with
questions.why: Reaching out to everyone makes sure no one is forgotten.

questions.q: A friend shares that they're struggling with their identity. What's the best response?
o: Listen, be supportive, and respect their privacy
questions.why: Listening and respecting privacy builds trust.

questions.q: You're asked to judge a competition where your friend is a participant. What's fair?
o: Declare the friendship and let someone else judge their entry
questions.why: Being open about conflicts of interest keeps things fair.

questions.q: Your group is stuck and nobody has new ideas. What helps?
o: Try a quick brainstorm where every idea is welcome
questions.why: Open brainstorming unlocks creativity.

questions.q: A classmate never says thanks when helped. How do you respond?
o: Keep helping if you can, and gently model gratitude
questions.why: Modelling good behaviour is more effective than demands.

questions.q: You overhear someone criticising your friend unfairly. What's best?
questions.why: Calmly offering another view is fair.

questions.q: You notice a quiet student is very knowledgeable. How can the class benefit?
o: Encourage them to share in small groups
Ask them to lead the whole class immediately
questions.why: Small groups help quiet experts share comfortably.

questions.q: You're working in a multicultural team and someone's festival falls during a deadline. What's respectful?
o: Adjust the plan together so they can celebrate
Let them skip without telling others
questions.why: Planning together respects everyone's traditions.

questions.q: A friend is upset that you shared a group photo they didn't like. What should you do?
o: Explain that everyone else liked it
questions.why: Respecting people's wishes about photos is important.

questions.q: You see a younger student being pressured by older ones. What's best?
o: Get a teacher right away, and stay near the younger student if it's safe
questions.why: Protecting younger students shows responsibility.

questions.q: In a team, credit and blame are often unfair. What's a good fix?
o: Agree on clear roles and track contributions
questions.why: Clear roles make credit and responsibility fair.

questions.q: Your classmates disagree on how to spend class funds. What's a fair process?
o: Collect ideas, discuss them openly, and vote
Spend it on the most popular idea immediately
questions.why: Open discussion and voting are fair.

questions.q: A friend keeps asking for favours but never returns them. What's healthy?
o: Politely set limits and say no sometimes
questions.why: Healthy limits protect friendships from resentment.

questions.q: You're paired with someone who has a learning difficulty. What's respectful?
o: Ask how they work best and adjust together
Speak slowly and loudly to them
questions.why: Asking how they work best shows respect.

questions.q: You're asked to speak for your group but disagree with their view. What's right?
o: Present the group's view fairly and share yours separately
questions.why: Fair representation is honest and respectful.

questions.q: Your group is celebrating a win. A member from a rival team looks upset. What's sporting?
questions.why: Acknowledging rivals is good sportsmanship.

questions.q: You join a new group and they have inside jokes you don't get. What helps?
o: Ask about them with good humour
questions.why: Asking with humour helps you connect.

questions.q: A classmate asks you to keep quiet about vandalism they did. What's right?
o: Encourage them to own up, and tell an adult if needed
questions.why: Encouraging honesty and involving adults is responsible.

questions.q: Your group disagrees about whether to include a struggling member. What's best?
o: Include them and give them a suitable role
Leave them out to save time
questions.why: Inclusion with the right role helps everyone.

questions.q: In your articleship team, a colleague keeps taking the easy tasks. What's the best approach?
o: Suggest fair task rotation in a team discussion
Do the hard tasks without a word
questions.why: Proposing fair rotation fixes the problem without blame.

questions.q: You're meeting a client for the first time. What helps build trust?
o: Listen to their concerns and explain clearly how you'll help
questions.why: Listening and clarity build client trust.

questions.q: Two teammates disagree on an audit approach. As senior, what do you do?
o: Hear both views, check the standards, and decide with reasons
Pick the approach of your favourite teammate
questions.why: Fair hearing plus reference to standards leads to sound decisions.

questions.q: A client's accountant is defensive during your audit queries. What's effective?
o: Explain that queries are routine and ask for their help
questions.why: Reducing defensiveness makes cooperation easier.

questions.q: You're new in a CA firm and don't know the office norms. What's best?
questions.why: Observing and asking helps you fit in professionally.

questions.q: Your manager asks you to work with a colleague you find difficult. What's professional?
o: Focus on shared goals and communicate clearly
Avoid them as much as possible
Ask to be reassigned at once
questions.why: Shared goals help difficult working relationships.

questions.q: A client asks you to bend a rule for them as a favour. What's right?
o: Politely decline and explain the professional standards
Agree to keep the client happy
questions.why: Professional ethics protect both you and the client.

questions.q: In a team call, a junior's idea is ignored. What can you do?
o: Bring the idea back and give them credit
Wait for them to repeat it
questions.why: Giving credit encourages juniors to contribute.

questions.q: You need information from another department that is slow to respond. What's best?
o: Follow up politely with a clear deadline and reason
questions.why: Polite follow-ups with clear needs get better results.

questions.q: Your colleague makes a mistake that the client noticed. What's the best team response?
o: Fix it together and present one apology as a team
Blame the colleague to the client
Let the colleague handle it alone
questions.why: Teams protect trust by fixing mistakes together.

questions.q: A batchmate is struggling with a topic you know well. What's a good step?
o: Offer to explain it in a short study session
questions.why: Helping peers builds a supportive network.

questions.q: You're asked to lead a small audit team for the first time. What's key?
o: Set clear roles, check in regularly, and listen to the team
Do most of the work yourself
Let everyone decide on their own
questions.why: Clear roles and listening make good leaders.

questions.q: A client invites you to a personal celebration. What's appropriate?
o: Thank them and follow your firm's policy on such invitations
questions.why: Following firm policy maintains independence and professionalism.

questions.q: Two clients are competitors and you work on both. What should you do?
o: Keep each client's information strictly confidential
questions.why: Confidentiality is a core professional duty.

questions.q: During a client meeting, your senior makes a factual error. What's best?
o: Mention it privately and quickly so it can be corrected
Correct them loudly in the meeting
questions.why: Private correction protects both the senior and the client.

questions.q: Your team is remote and communication is poor. What helps?
o: Set a short daily check-in and shared task list
Call each person whenever you like
questions.why: Regular check-ins and shared lists keep teams aligned.

questions.q: A client is confused by your report. What's best?
o: Walk them through it in simple language
Tell them to read it carefully
questions.why: Simple explanations help clients understand.

questions.q: You notice a colleague is excluded from team lunches. What can you do?
o: Ask others why they exclude them
questions.why: A simple invitation makes people feel included.

questions.q: You disagree with a client's accounting treatment. How do you raise it?
o: Explain the standard and its impact respectfully, with evidence
Accept it to keep the client
questions.why: Evidence-based respectful discussion is professional.

questions.q: Your articleship partner wants to split tasks unfairly. What's the best response?
o: Propose a fair split based on time and skill
questions.why: A fair proposal solves the issue directly.

questions.q: In a negotiation on audit fees, the client pushes back hard. What's effective?
o: Explain the value and scope, and look for a fair middle ground
questions.why: Explaining value and seeking fairness builds long-term relationships.

questions.q: You hear office gossip about a colleague. What's the professional response?
o: Don't spread it and steer the conversation away
Tell the colleague what's being said
questions.why: Not spreading gossip keeps the workplace respectful.

questions.q: A colleague from another city joins your team. What helps them settle in?
o: Introduce them to the team and offer help with local things
Tell them office stories about others
questions.why: Welcoming new colleagues helps them settle quickly.

questions.q: A client shares sensitive personal information during tax filing. What should you do?
o: Keep it confidential and use it only for the work
Share it with your team for interest
Note it in your personal diary
Mention it casually to other clients
questions.why: Confidentiality is a professional and legal duty.

questions.q: Your team missed a deadline because of a client's delay. How do you tell your manager?
o: Explain the facts, the impact, and the new plan
questions.why: Facts with a plan show professionalism.

questions.q: Your study group has one member who dominates. What's a fair solution?
o: Agree on a rotation where each person leads a topic
questions.why: Rotation gives everyone a chance.

questions.q: A client offers you a gift during the audit. What's right?
o: Politely decline or follow the firm's gift policy
Tell the client it's a bribe
questions.why: Following gift policies protects independence.

questions.q: In a meeting, two partners disagree and ask for your view. What's best?
questions.why: Fact-based views are respected.

questions.q: You need to deliver bad news to a client about a penalty. What's best?
o: Explain clearly, early, with options to reduce impact
questions.why: Early, clear communication with options helps clients.

questions.q: A colleague asks for your help but you're very busy. What's professional?
o: Explain your workload and suggest a time or another person
Help immediately and miss your deadline
questions.why: Honest, helpful responses maintain good relationships.

questions.q: You're giving feedback to a peer on their working papers. What's most useful?
o: Specific points with examples and suggestions
questions.why: Specific feedback is easiest to act on.

questions.q: A client's staff speak a different language. How do you communicate better?
o: Use simple words, visuals, and check understanding
questions.why: Simple words and checks prevent misunderstandings.

questions.q: You see a colleague taking shortcuts in documentation. What's right?
o: Raise it with them, and tell your senior if it continues
questions.why: Addressing it directly helps maintain quality.

questions.q: Your team celebrates a successful audit. One member was on leave but did key prep. What's fair?
o: Mention their contribution in the celebration
questions.why: Recognising all contributors is fair.

questions.q: A client wants weekly updates but your firm usually sends monthly. What's best?
o: Agree on a frequency that suits both, and document it
questions.why: Agreeing expectations prevents conflict.

questions.q: You're asked to train new articles. What's a good approach?
o: Explain the why behind tasks and give practice
Let them learn by mistakes alone
questions.why: Understanding the why speeds up learning.

questions.q: Your team has a difficult client call. Who should speak?
o: Agree in advance who leads each topic
questions.why: Planning roles makes calls smoother.

questions.q: A client compliments one team member only. What should you do?
o: Share the compliment and credit the whole team's effort
Tell the client others did more
questions.why: Sharing credit builds team morale.

questions.q: You have a conflict of interest with a new client. What's right?
o: Disclose it to your firm right away
Ask the client what to do
questions.why: Disclosure protects integrity.

questions.q: A peer is struggling emotionally during exam season. What can you do?
o: Check in, listen, and encourage them to seek support
questions.why: Supportive peers make a big difference.

questions.q: Your firm's partner prefers formal communication. How do you adjust?
o: Write clear, formal emails and reports
questions.why: Adapting to communication styles shows professionalism.

questions.q: You're at a networking event and know nobody. What's a good start?
o: Introduce yourself to someone standing alone
Wait for someone to approach you
questions.why: Approaching someone alone is easy and kind.

questions.q: A client asks you something outside your knowledge. What's best?
o: Say you'll check and get back by a set time
questions.why: Honest follow-up builds credibility.

questions.q: Your team member shares a personal problem affecting work. What's supportive?
o: Listen, offer flexibility if possible, and keep it private
questions.why: Support and privacy build trust.

questions.q: In a joint audit with another firm, there's disagreement on findings. What's best?
o: Discuss the evidence together; if you still differ, document it and report as joint-audit rules require
questions.why: Evidence-based discussion leads to sound conclusions.

questions.q: You find a better way to do a routine task. What's the team-friendly step?
o: Share it with the team and show how it works
Keep it for yourself to look good
questions.why: Sharing improvements helps everyone.

questions.q: A colleague takes all the client calls and you never get to speak. What should you do?
o: Ask to lead a part of the next call
questions.why: Asking for a role helps you grow professionally.

questions.q: Your friend wants to copy your homework because they forgot. What's the best way to help?
o: Explain the main idea quickly so they can do it themselves
Let them copy just this once since they forgot
Tell the teacher before class that they forgot
Say no and walk off without explaining
questions.why: Helping them understand is kinder and fair to everyone.

questions.q: Your group of friends always speaks in a language one member doesn't understand. What should you do?
o: Suggest everyone uses a language all of you know
Keep talking, they will learn it eventually
Translate only the important parts later
Tell that member to find other friends
questions.why: Using a shared language keeps everyone included.

questions.q: Your debate partner wants to use a fact you know is wrong. What do you do?
o: Tell them privately and find a correct source together
Use it anyway because the judges may not notice
Let them use it and say it was their idea
Refuse to debate with them at all
questions.why: Fixing the fact together protects your team's honesty.

questions.q: Your friend group makes a decision while you were away and it affects you. What's best?
o: Tell them calmly you'd like to be included in such decisions
Accept it and stay quiet to avoid trouble
Undo the decision without asking anyone
Leave the group the same day
questions.why: Calmly asking to be included sets a fair expectation.

questions.q: You and a classmate are competing for the same scholarship. They ask for help with a form. What's right?
o: Help them with the form honestly
Give them slightly wrong advice to stay ahead
Say you're busy every time they ask
Help them only if they help you more
questions.why: Competing fairly means you don't hold others back.

questions.q: A teacher praises your group, but you know one member barely helped. What's fair?
o: Discuss it with the group and agree to share work better next time
Tell the teacher in front of the class
Say nothing and let it go forever
Exclude that member from the next project
questions.why: Fixing the pattern within the team is fair and kind.

questions.q: Someone shares your private message in a group without asking. How do you respond?
o: Tell them privately that it hurt your trust and ask them not to repeat it
Share one of their private messages in return
Leave every group they are in
questions.why: Clear, private feedback protects your boundaries.

questions.q: At a school event, guests from another school are standing alone. As a host, what do you do?
o: Welcome them and show them where to sit and eat
Wait for a teacher to look after them
Point them to the notice board
questions.why: Good hosts make guests feel welcome.

questions.q: Your friend keeps checking their phone while you talk. What's a good way to raise it?
o: Say lightly, "Can I have your attention for a minute?"
questions.why: A light, direct request usually works without a fight.

questions.q: In a team, you are the only one who disagrees with a risky plan. What should you do?
o: State your concern clearly once with reasons, then help reduce the risk
Stay silent to keep the peace
Keep arguing until they give up
questions.why: Speaking up clearly and then helping makes the team safer.

questions.q: A classmate says your community's food is "weird". What's a good reply?
o: "It's different from yours. Want to try some?"
Report them to the principal immediately
questions.why: Inviting curiosity turns a rude comment into understanding.

questions.q: You notice the same three people always get chosen for school events. What could you suggest?
o: A fair rotation so more students get a chance
questions.why: Rotation gives everyone a fair chance to grow.

questions.q: Your senior asks you to sign a working paper for a test you didn't perform. What's right?
o: Politely refuse and offer to perform the test now
Sign it since the senior asked
Sign it and mention it later
Ask a colleague to sign instead
questions.why: Signing only for work you did is a basic professional rule.

questions.q: A client's staff member is rude to your junior during fieldwork. What do you do?
o: Address it calmly with the client's manager and support your junior
Tell your junior to ignore it
Be rude back to the staff member
questions.why: Calmly protecting your team keeps the work professional.

questions.q: Your firm uses a new collaboration tool and some seniors resist it. How can you help?
o: Offer a short demo showing how it saves them time
Report them for not using it
Use it alone and ignore them
questions.why: Showing the benefit helps people adopt change.
